title: Maori middens

paragraphs.text: Now turn to section four on page six.
Section four.
You will hear part of a lecture about archaeological diggings in New Zealand. First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty on page seven.
Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the lecture.
Today, I'm going to be asking the question: What can archaeologists learn from studying middens?
'Midden' is an Old English word meaning a domestic rubbish dump.
By way of providing a local New Zealand example, let me tell you about an ancient midden I excavated recently that was made by the Maori people in this country.

It consisted primarily of leftovers from meals, particularly a great quantity of shells from seafood. I also came across something very exciting, an ax that had been discarded because it was damaged. Finds of this kind are of great interest because they tell us about the technologies developed by people in the past.
For the same reason, I was most pleased to unearth several fish hooks, another item commonly found in Maori middens.
Their hooks were manufactured using bone, which is a durable material that can last for hundreds of years in the right conditions.

But why is rubbish like this important, you might well ask? Well, the reason archaeologists are fascinated by rubbish is that it provides information about ordinary life, and written history doesn't always do that.
Now, having whetted your appetite for middens, I should just mention that they are protected by law.
If you wish to make any excavation at a midden, you must first obtain a permit from the Historic Places Trust. It is an offense to work on a midden without doing this.
So how can you find a midden? The best place is on the beach or among sand dunes. Look for low mounds of shells.
Some sort of erosion is often important because middens were usually buried.
For this reason, it's not uncommon to find a midden where a road is being constructed and the contractors are digging into the land.

Now, in the past, we could only make rough estimates regarding the age of a midden. But with modern radiocarbon dating techniques, archaeologists can accurately ascertain the date it was made. It's even possible to establish what season of the year the midden was created. This may not sound like useful information at first, but it actually gives us an insight into Maori migration, when and where they traveled.

What else can we discover from middens? Well, we can learn a great deal about diet. For example, the study of middens has revealed that the Maori people who lived here before Europeans arrived first concentrated their hunting on giant birds, which were rich in fat. But later, as this resource became scarce, they had to find an alternative, so mostly turned to fish, which of course, has a much lower fat content.

This kind of discovery is most useful because it allows us to speculate about how healthy people were and also what life expectancy the population could look forward to at different stages of its history.
Well, I'm now going to talk about different varieties of middens. The most common type in this country are those made up of shells, which of course, are found close to beaches.
The other thing to remember with shell middens is that New Zealand has several species of freshwater mussels, as well as the much more common saltwater varieties.
This means that small middens made up of these shells are occasionally found beside lakes, which can be hundreds of kilometers from the sea in quite mountainous areas.

Middens containing no shell material have occasionally been discovered in various regions of the South Island, particularly Central Otago and on the East Coast. However, the thing to emphasize here is that they are extremely rare.
I don't know of any new discoveries in the last ten years.

Finally, middens dating from the early European period of New Zealand's history are also fascinating. How can we distinguish European and Maori middens? Well, certain items are only found in European middens, notably things made of glass, which was a material unknown to Maori.
But in other respects, the two types are often remarkably similar, suggesting that in many ways, the first European settlers adapted to the Maori way of life.

One other distinguishing feature I should just mention is that the two types of middens tend to be found in different locations. Historic European middens are less restricted to the coastlines, and particularly large ones have been left behind in places where soldiers had their camps. Well, that's the end of the formal part of the lecture.
That is the end of section four. You now have half a minute to check your answers.
